source_refs.quote: sub-let, assigned or otherwise parted with the possession
These three expressions deal with different concepts and apply to different circumstances.

In subletting there exists the relationship of landlord and tenant as between the tenant and his sub-tenant and all the incidents of letting or tenancy have to be found, namely the transfer of an interest in the estate payment of rent, and the right to possession as against the tenant in respect of the Premises sublet.
In assignment the tenant has to divest himself of all the rights that he has as a tenant.
there must be vesting of possession by the tenant in another person by divesting himself not only of physical possession but also of the right to possession
The divestment or abandonment of the right to possession is necessary in order to invoke the clause of parting with possession
If there is anything in the nature of a right to concurrent user there is no parting with possession
The mere user by other persons is no parting with Possession so long as the tenant retains the legal possession himself

source_refs.quote: the said tenant Sh. Ramesh Kumar had parted with possession and sub-let and assigned the same initially to one Sh. Ghanshyam Dass and subsequently to Sh. Bhagwan Dass, who were his father and brother respectively.

nodes.text: It was alleged that tenant Sh. Ramesh Kumar parted with possession of, sub-let, and assigned the premises initially to Sh. Ghanshyam Dass and subsequently to Sh. Bhagwan Dass

source_refs.quote: the said tenant Sh. Ramesh Kumar had parted with possession and sub-let and assigned the same initially to one Sh. Ghanshyam Dass and subsequently to Sh. Bhagwan Dass, who were his father and brother respectively.

nodes.text: Bhagwant Dass was pleaded to be opening and closing the shop and dealing with customers

source_refs.quote: The current sub-lessee Bhagwant Dass was pleaded to be opening and closing the shop and dealing with the customers.

nodes.text: It was denied that the property had been sub-let to Sh. Bhagwan Dass

source_refs.quote: it was denied that the property had been sub let by him to his brother Bhagwan Dass.

nodes.text: It was asserted that Sh. Bhagwan Dass was helping in opening and closing the shop and dealing with customers

source_refs.quote: his brother Bhagwan Dass was helping him in opening and closing the shop and dealing with the customers.

nodes.text: It was denied that Sh. Bhagwan Dass was a sub-tenant in the suit premises

source_refs.quote: However, it was denied that Sh. Bhagwan Dass was a sub tenant in the suit premises.

nodes.text: Both witnesses deposed that Sh. Bhagwan Dass was running the shop

source_refs.quote: Both the witnesses deposed that Sh. Bhagwan Dass was running the shop and not respondent Sh. Ramesh Kumar.

nodes.text: Both witnesses deposed that respondent Sh. Ramesh Kumar was not running the shop

source_refs.quote: Both the witnesses deposed that Sh. Bhagwan Dass was running the shop and not respondent Sh. Ramesh Kumar.

nodes.text: Both witnesses deposed that Sh. Bhagwan Dass was working as an employee and drawing a salary of Rs. 10,000 per month

source_refs.quote: Both the witnesses deposed that Sh. Bhagwan Dass was working as an employee and drawing a salary of Rs. 10,000/- per month.

nodes.text: It was admitted that Sh. Bhagwan Dass operated the shop and possessed its key

source_refs.quote: The fact of Sh. Bhagwan Dass operating the shop and being in possession of key thereof was admitted.

nodes.text: The trial court found that the brother's use of the premises was only a privilege or licence that could be terminated at the respondent's will

source_refs.quote: Trial court held that it was only a privilege or a licence by the tenant in favour of his brother to use the premises, which licence or privilege could be terminated at the sweet will and pleasure of respondent.

nodes.text: The trial court found that Bhagwan Dass was a family member rather than a stranger or outsider and that sub-letting could not be inferred

source_refs.quote: Further, it was the trial court's view that Bhagwan Dass was not a stranger or outsider but a family member of the respondent, therefore, sub-letting cannot be inferred.

nodes.text: Witness testimony recorded that Sh. Bhagwan Dass was running the shop and respondent Sh. Ramesh Kumar was not

source_refs.quote: Both the witnesses deposed that Sh. Bhagwan Dass was running the shop and not respondent Sh. Ramesh Kumar.

nodes.text: The current sub-lessee Bhagwant Dass was pleaded to be opening and closing the shop and dealing with the customers. It was also pleaded that the aforesaid Sh. nodes.text: 2.1 Petition was resisted by present respondent - tenant Sh. Ramesh Kumar and it was denied that the property had been sub let by him to his brother Bhagwan Dass. It was pleaded by the respondent that he is occupying the demised shop as a tenant and additionally conducting his business from shop no. 5765, Sikli Gran, Factory Road, Nabi Karim, New Delhi-110055.

source_refs.quote: 2.1 Petition was resisted by present respondent - tenant Sh. Ramesh Kumar and it was denied that the property had been sub let by him to his brother Bhagwan Dass. It was pleaded by the respondent that he is occupying the demised shop as a tenant and additionally conducting his business from shop no. 5765, Sikli Gran, Factory Road, Nabi Karim, New Delhi-110055.

nodes.text: As regards the respondent's brother Bhagwan Dass, it was further case of the respondent that his brother Bhagwan Dass was helping him in opening and closing the shop and dealing with the customers. However, it was denied that Sh. Bhagwan Dass was a sub tenant in the suit premises. Petitioner was pleaded to be receiving rent from the respondent.

nodes.text: 3. Petitioner in support of her case examined her attorney, Sh. M.L. Jain as PW-1, who supported the petition. Petitioner also examined two other witnesses, who were shopkeepers having their shops in the vicinity. Both the witnesses deposed that Sh. Bhagwan Dass was running the shop and not respondent Sh. Ramesh Kumar.

source_refs.quote: 3. Petitioner in support of her case examined her attorney, Sh. M.L. Jain as PW-1, who supported the petition. Petitioner also examined two other witnesses, who were shopkeepers having their shops in the vicinity. Both the witnesses deposed that Sh. Bhagwan Dass was running the shop and not respondent Sh. Ramesh Kumar.

nodes.text: 4. Respondent in support of his case examined himself as RW-1 and his brother Sh. Bhagwan Dass, the alleged sub-lessee, as RW-2. Both the witnesses deposed that Sh. Bhagwan Dass was working as an employee and drawing a salary of Rs. 10,000/- per month. The fact of Sh. Bhagwan Dass operating the shop and being in possession of key thereof was admitted. No proof of any other employee was produced. Salary vouchers of payment of salary to Sh. Bhagwan Dass were also not proved.

source_refs.quote: 4. Respondent in support of his case examined himself as RW-1 and his brother Sh. Bhagwan Dass, the alleged sub-lessee, as RW-2. Both the witnesses deposed that Sh. Bhagwan Dass was working as an employee and drawing a salary of Rs. 10,000/- per month. The fact of Sh. Bhagwan Dass operating the shop and being in possession of key thereof was admitted. No proof of any other employee was produced. Salary vouchers of payment of salary to Sh. Bhagwan Dass were also not proved.

nodes.text: 5. Trial Court by the impugned judgment took the view that the fact of sub tenancy was not established. Trial court held that it was only a privilege or a licence by the tenant in favour of his brother to use the premises, which licence or privilege could be terminated at the sweet will and pleasure of respondent. Therefore, the arrangement did not amount to assignment or parting with the possession.

source_refs.quote: 5. Trial Court by the impugned judgment took the view that the fact of sub tenancy was not established. Trial court held that it was only a privilege or a licence by the tenant in favour of his brother to use the premises, which licence or privilege could be terminated at the sweet will and pleasure of respondent. Therefore, the arrangement did not amount to assignment or parting with the possession.

nodes.text: Further, it was the trial court's view that Bhagwan Dass was not a stranger or outsider but a family member of the respondent, therefore, sub-letting cannot be inferred.

source_refs.quote: If there is anything in the nature of a right to concurrent user there is no parting with possession
The mere user by other persons is no parting with Possession so long as the tenant retains the legal possession himself
A tenant cannot be said to part with the possession of any part of the premises unless his agreement with the license wholly ousts him from the legal possession of that part.

source_refs.quote: If there is anything in the nature of a right to concurrent user there is no parting with possession
The mere user by other persons is no parting with Possession so long as the tenant retains the legal possession himself
A tenant cannot be said to part with the possession of any part of the premises unless his agreement with the license wholly ousts him from the legal possession of that part.

Notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in any other law or contract, no order or decree for the recovery of possession of any premises shall be made by any court or Controller in favour of the landlord against a tenant:Provided that the Controller may, on an application made to him in the prescribed manner, make an order for the recovery of possession of the premises on one or more of the following grounds only, namely: -

IK-190902:L107.text: 30. So long as the lessee retains the legal possession of the whole of the premises he does not commit a breach of law against parting with the possession by allowing other people to use the same. A tenant cannot be said to part with the possession of any part of the premises unless his agreement with the license wholly ousts him from the legal possession of that part. If there is anything in the nature of a right to concurrent user there is no parting with possession: See Stenina v.

IK-190902:L108.text: Abrahama, (1931) f Ch D 470 and G. D. Chaudhary v. Anand Sarup. 1966 Delhi Lt 28.

IK-190902:L109.text: 31. Clause (b) of the proviso to cite8†Section 14(1) uses three expressions namely 'sublet', 'assign' and 'otherwise parted with the possession of the whole or any part of the premises without obtaining the consent in writing of the landlord'. These three expressions deal with different concepts and apply to different circumstances.

IK-190902:L110.text: In subletting there exists the relationship of landlord and tenant as between the tenant and his sub-tenant and all the incidents of letting or tenancy have to be found, namely the transfer of an interest in the estate payment of rent, and the right to possession as against the tenant in respect of the Premises sublet. In assignment the tenant has to divest himself of all the rights that he has as a tenant.

IK-190902:L111.text: The expression "parted with possession" undoubtedly postulates parting with possession session means giving possession to persons other than those to whom possession has been given by lease and "parting with possession" must have been by the tenant.

IK-190902:L112.text: The mere user by other persons is no parting with Possession so long as the tenant retains the legal possession himself or in other words there must be vesting of possession by the tenant in another person by divesting himself not only of physical possession but also of the right to possession. The divestment or abandonment of the right to possession is necessary in order to invoke the clause of parting with possession: See cite11†Hazari Lal v. Gian Ram . 1972 Ren Cr 74 (Delhi).
